lead: This unit explains how a matched transistor pair amplifies the difference between two inputs and rejects the signal common to both. It then builds current mirrors, active loads and the internal stages of an op-amp, and shows how real op-amp parameters and compensation shape performance. After the unit, you can analyse a differential amplifier, estimate CMRR, design a simple current mirror, and read a two-stage CMOS op-amp or OTA at block and small-signal level.
about: The unit opens with the matched differential pair, the circuit that turns a difference between two inputs into a current. Chapter 5.2 separates differential and common-mode gain and defines CMRR. Chapter 5.3 builds current mirrors that supply the tail bias and later act as loads. Chapter 5.4 uses those mirrors as active loads to raise gain in a CMOS differential amplifier. Chapter 5.5 assembles the input, gain, level-shifter and output stages of an op-amp. Chapter 5.6 measures the real op-amp's offset, bias current, slew rate and PSRR. Chapter 5.7 compensates a two-stage CMOS op-amp for stable feedback. Chapter 5.8 presents the OTA, a bias-tunable transconductance stage.

chapters.idea: A matched pair with a tail current source steers current in proportion to the input difference, so it amplifies a difference and ignores a common signal.
chapters.depth: Start from the long-tailed pair: two matched BJTs with emitters joined to a tail current source IEE, or two MOSFETs with sources joined. Define vid = v1 − v2 and vicm = (v1 + v2)/2. At vid = 0, each device carries IEE/2. For small vid, the change in each collector or drain current is ±gm vid/2; gm = IC/VT for a BJT and gm = 2ID/VOV for a MOSFET. Show differential output at the two collectors or drains and single-ended output at one collector or drain. Treat the joined emitter or source node as a virtual ground for differential signals and as a follower for common-mode signals. Explain why a current-source tail gives high common-mode rejection. Some syllabi call this the emitter-coupled pair, source-coupled pair or long-tailed pair. Keep mismatch and CMRR for 5.2.

figure.title: Differential pair: current steering
figure.aria: Block diagram: a tail current source biases a matched pair; the input difference steers the tail current between the two devices to form the output.

chapters.example: A BJT differential pair has IEE = 1 mA, VCC = 12 V, RC = 5 kΩ on each collector, and VT = 26 mV. β is very large. (a) Find IC1 and IC2 at vid = 0. (b) Find gm and the single-ended differential gain at collector 1. (c) For vid = 5 mV, find vC1, vC2 and the differential output voltage.
chapters.trap: Using IC = IEE instead of IEE/2 at balance; forgetting the 1/2 factor for a single-ended output; treating the emitter or source node as a virtual ground for common-mode signals.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: BJT and MOSFET biasing, small-signal gm and rπ or ro.
chapters.leave: CMRR and common-mode gain to 5.2; current-mirror design to 5.3; active loads to 5.4.

chapters.idea: Any two inputs split into a differential part and a common-mode part; the amplifier should multiply the first and reject the second, measured by CMRR.
chapters.depth: Define differential-mode gain Ad = vod/vid and common-mode gain Acm = voc/vicm. Use v1 = vicm + vid/2 and v2 = vicm − vid/2. For a BJT pair with tail resistance REE and collector resistor RC, single-ended Acm ≈ −RC/(2REE); with an ideal current source Acm is set by mismatch. CMRR = |Ad/Acm|; in dB, CMRR = 20 log10 |Ad/Acm|. For a single-ended BJT pair, Ad = gm RC/2, so CMRR ≈ REE/re. Cover resistor mismatch: a fractional mismatch δRC/RC gives Acm/Ad roughly δRC/RC for a differential output. Define common-mode input range. Some syllabi call CMRR the common-mode rejection ratio. Keep op-amp PSRR for 5.6.

figure.title: Splitting inputs into difference and common mode
figure.aria: Block diagram: inputs v1 and v2 are split into a difference vid and an average vicm, which pass through separate gains Ad and Acm before adding at the output.

chapters.example: An amplifier has differential gain Ad = 200, CMRR = 80 dB, v1 = 1.010 V and v2 = 0.990 V. Find vid, vicm, Acm, the differential output, the common-mode output, and the worst-case total output magnitude.
chapters.trap: Putting vid = v1 + v2 or vicm = v1 + v2; using 10 log instead of 20 log for CMRR in dB; thinking CMRR is a difference of gains.
chapters.leave: Op-amp CMRR measurement to 5.6; detailed mismatch analysis to 5.7 if needed.

chapters.idea: A transistor plus a reference current copies that current into another branch; the copy is set by geometry ratio and improved by high output resistance.
chapters.depth: BJT mirror: diode-connected Q1 sets VBE; matched Q2 copies IC. IREF = (VCC − VBE)/R. With finite β, IOUT = IREF/(1 + 2/β); base currents cause the error. Emitter resistors improve matching. Wilson and cascode mirrors raise output resistance; a Widlar source gives small currents. MOSFET mirror: IOUT/IREF = (W/L)2/(W/L)1 when VGS is shared; channel-length modulation gives ro = 1/(λID) and a finite output resistance. Define compliance voltage as the minimum VOUT that keeps the mirror in saturation or active region. Show the current source as tail bias for a differential pair. Some syllabi call these current mirror circuits. Keep active-load use for 5.4.

figure.title: Basic current mirror
figure.aria: Block diagram: a reference current flows through a diode-connected transistor, sets a gate or base voltage, and a second matched transistor copies the current to the output.

chapters.example: Using a 5 V supply, design a simple BJT current mirror for an output current of about 1 mA. VBE = 0.7 V, β = 100, VA = 50 V. Find R for IREF = 1 mA, the actual IOUT, and ro.
chapters.trap: Ignoring base-current error 2/β; expecting IOUT to stay fixed when VOUT changes; inverting the W/L ratio; forgetting the minimum output voltage or compliance limit.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: BJT and MOSFET bias circuits; 5.1 tail source.
chapters.leave: Active-load use to 5.4; op-amp bias chain to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Replacing load resistors with a current-mirror load raises the small-signal output resistance and converts a differential input into a single-ended output with much higher gain.
chapters.depth: In a CMOS pair, an NMOS differential pair has a PMOS current-mirror load. The mirror copies the current change of one side into the other, so a differential input becomes a single-ended output current of gm1 vid. The output resistance is ro_n || ro_p, giving Ad = gm1 (ro_n || ro_p). This is much larger than gm RD/2 from a resistor load. The tail current source keeps common-mode gain low. Show the five-transistor OTA core. Some syllabi call this an active-loaded differential amplifier or CMOS OTA. Keep two-stage design for 5.7.

figure.title: CMOS pair with active load
figure.aria: Block diagram: a tail current biases an NMOS pair, a PMOS mirror acts as the load, and the mirror converts the differential current into a single-ended high-gain output.

chapters.example: A CMOS differential pair with a current-mirror active load has gm1 = 1 mS, ro_n = 100 kΩ, ro_p = 50 kΩ, and tail current 200 µA. Find Rout and the differential gain. Compare with a 10 kΩ resistor load per side and single-ended output.
chapters.trap: Using gm RD/2 for an active load; thinking the mirror load halves the gain; forgetting that a mirror load also converts differential to single-ended.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.3; Unit 2 MOSFET small-signal output resistance.
chapters.leave: Two-stage op-amp and compensation to 5.7; OTA to 5.8.

chapters.idea: An op-amp is a chain of four functions: a differential input stage, a high-gain stage, a level shifter that moves the DC level without losing gain, and an output buffer that drives load current.
chapters.depth: Walk through the four internal functions. Input stage: differential pair with active load; it sets input resistance, offset and CMRR. Gain stage: CE or CS with active load; it gives most voltage gain and is the place for Miller compensation. Level shifter: emitter follower or source follower with a current source, or a resistor divider; it shifts the DC level down without changing the signal much. Output stage: class AB push-pull buffer; it gives low output resistance and current drive, with short-circuit current limiting. The overall gain is the product of stage gains. Some syllabi call the gain stage the intermediate stage and the output stage the output buffer. Use the 741 as a common example but leave device-by-device bias analysis to advanced reading.

figure.title: Op-amp internal chain
figure.aria: Block diagram: the op-amp signal passes from a differential input stage to a gain stage, a level shifter, and an output buffer before reaching the load.

chapters.example: An op-amp has input-stage gain Av1 = 100, gain-stage gain Av2 = 500, level-shifter gain 0.5, and output-buffer gain 0.98. Find the open-loop gain in V/V and dB. For vid = 1 mV, find the ideal output and say whether a ±12 V supply clips it.
chapters.trap: Adding gains in dB incorrectly; thinking the level shifter gives gain; assuming the output can reach the supply rails; ignoring output current limit.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.4; Unit 4 negative feedback for closed-loop later.
chapters.leave: Exact 741 bias analysis to advanced reading; parameters to 5.6; compensation to 5.7.

chapters.idea: Real op-amps depart from the ideal in DC, through offset voltage and bias current, and in large-signal or high-frequency behaviour, through slew rate and PSRR.
chapters.depth: Define input offset voltage Vos as the differential DC input that makes Vout = 0. Define IB = (IB+ + IB−)/2 and IOS = |IB+ − IB−|. Show how Vos and IB create output errors: for a unity-gain buffer, Vos appears directly; IB through a resistor R gives IB R. Slew rate SR = max dVout/dt; in a two-stage op-amp SR = I5/Cc. Full-power bandwidth FPBW = SR/(2π Vpeak). PSRR = ΔVos/ΔVsupply or 20 log10 |Ad/Asupply|; define the sign convention used. Cover output swing, input common-mode range and temperature drift. Mention that CMRR was defined in 5.2. Keep compensation for 5.7.

figure.title: Non-ideal op-amp error sources
figure.aria: Block diagram: input mismatch creates Vos and IOS, supply changes create PSRR error, and the compensation capacitor limits slew rate; all three affect the output error and limits.

chapters.example: An op-amp has SR = 0.5 V/µs and Cc = 30 pF. It is used as a unity-gain buffer with a 2 V step. Find the slewing time to 2 V, the full-power bandwidth for a 2 V peak sine wave, and the current charging Cc.
chapters.trap: Mixing V/µs with V/s; using peak-to-peak instead of peak in FPBW; confusing PSRR with CMRR; treating offset current as bias current.
chapters.leave: Compensation design to 5.7; op-amp applications to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A two-stage CMOS op-amp has two poles; Miller compensation splits them so the amplifier is stable in feedback, at the cost of bandwidth and slew rate.
chapters.depth: Two-stage CMOS op-amp: first stage is the active-loaded differential pair with transconductance Gm1; second stage is a common-source amplifier with transconductance Gm2 and output resistance R2. Add Cc from the second-stage output back to the first-stage output. Miller compensation makes the dominant pole p1 ≈ 1/(Gm2 R1 R2 Cc) and pushes the second pole to p2 ≈ Gm2/C2. The unity-gain frequency is f_u ≈ Gm1/(2π Cc). For 60° phase margin, place p2 at least about 2.2 times f_u; a common design target is 3 times. The right-half-plane zero at Gm2/Cc is moved with a nulling resistor Rz = 1/Gm2. Slew rate SR = I5/Cc, so SR = 2π f_u VOV; this is the transition-frequency to slew-rate relation some syllabi use. Gm reduction with source degeneration allows a smaller Cc for the same f_u and hence a higher SR; only a few universities teach this method in detail. Keep folded cascode for advanced reading.

figure.aria: Bode magnitude plot: the compensated op-amp has a dominant pole near 10 Hz, unity gain near 10 kHz, and a second pole near 100 kHz that bends the curve to a steeper roll-off.

chapters.example: A two-stage CMOS op-amp has Gm1 = 1 mS, I5 = 200 µA, Cc = 2 pF, and C2 = 5 pF. Find the unity-gain frequency, the slew rate, and the minimum Gm2 for a second pole at 3 times the unity-gain frequency.
chapters.trap: Using Cc as the load capacitor; forgetting Miller multiplication; placing the compensation capacitor across the wrong stage; ignoring the right-half-plane zero.
chapters.prereq: 5.4, 5.5 and 5.6; Unit 3 poles and phase margin.
chapters.leave: Folded-cascode op-amp to advanced reading; filter design to Unit 7.

chapters.idea: An OTA is a voltage-controlled current source: its output current is proportional to the differential input voltage, with transconductance Gm set by an external bias current.
chapters.depth: Define the OTA as Iout = Gm(v+ − v−). It has a high output resistance and no output buffer. For a simple CMOS pair, Gm = IBIAS/VOV = √(2k′(W/L)ID) with ID = IBIAS/2. The linear input range is about ±VOV; beyond that the square-law, or tanh for a BJT pair, makes Gm fall. The transconductance is tunable by IBIAS, so the OTA is used in Gm-C filters, variable-gain amplifiers and oscillators. Compare with an op-amp: voltage output, low output resistance, fixed closed-loop gain set by feedback. Some OTAs add an output buffer. Only a few universities teach OTA design as a separate topic. Keep filter synthesis for Unit 7.

figure.title: OTA as a tunable transconductor
figure.aria: Block diagram: bias current IBIAS sets transconductance Gm, the input difference vid controls the output current Iout, and the output has high resistance so it behaves as a current source.

chapters.example: A simple CMOS OTA has k′ = 100 µA/V², W/L = 25, IBIAS = 100 µA, and VOV = 0.2 V. Find Gm, Iout for vid = 10 mV, and the approximate linear input range.
chapters.trap: Confusing Gm with open-loop voltage gain; using the small-signal Iout formula outside the linear range; forgetting that Gm changes with IBIAS.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 and 5.4; Unit 7 Gm-C filters if taught.
chapters.leave: Gm-C filter design to Unit 7; op-amp voltage applications to Unit 6.
